---
title: "Set 15 — random forests and gradient boosting"
subtitle: "After lecture 17 · 27 November · about 45 minutes"
---

Data: [`churn.csv`](../materials/churn.csv), the same split as Set 14
(`set.seed(1)`, 70/30, `id` dropped).

Before you start: `set.seed(15)` right before every `ranger()`, `xgb.cv()` and
`xgboost()` call — the Blackboard test checks your numbers against this seed.
Forest and boosting results shift a little between package versions; the test
allows for that.

## 1 · One tree, then five hundred

Fit a random forest (`ranger`, `num.trees = 500`, `probability = TRUE`) and
compare AUC against your pruned tree from last week.

Where did the improvement come from? Answer with the word *variance* and explain
what averaging does to it.

## 2 · What `mtry` is for

Refit with `mtry` equal to 2, to the default, and to the number of predictors.

The last one has a name — it is no longer a random forest. Which method is it,
and why does forcing every split to see every variable make the trees *more*
alike and the ensemble *worse*?

## 3 · Boosting is a different idea [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 18, on 30 Nov — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Fit gradient boosting (`xgboost` or `gbm`) with a small learning rate and enough
rounds, using early stopping on a validation fold.

Forests average trees fitted independently; boosting fits each tree on what is
left over. Write three sentences that would let a colleague choose between them
without using the words "usually better".

## 4 · The overfitting each one can and cannot do

Push both to an extreme: the forest to 2 000 trees, the boosting to 5 000 rounds
with no early stopping.

One of them degrades and one does not. Report which, and explain the asymmetry —
it is the most useful single fact in this lecture.

## 5 · Importance, and its price [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 18, on 30 Nov — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Extract variable importance from the forest, and SHAP or gain from the boosting.

Do the top three agree? Then answer the question a manager will ask: *"so if we
change that variable, does churn fall?"* The honest answer is one sentence, and
it is not yes.

## Check yourself on Blackboard

Open the test **Set 15** on Blackboard and enter your numbers. Feedback appears
as soon as you submit. Nothing is graded, and you can take it as many times as
you like.

---

*This set checks: variance reduction versus sequential correction, why early
stopping matters for one and not the other, and that importance is not
causation.*
